# Impact of modernizing eligibility criteria on enrollment and representation in acute myeloid leukemia clinical trials

**Authors:** Andrew Hantel; Yating Wang; Angel Cronin; Irum Khan; Ivy Abraham; Ann-Kathrin Eisfeld; Anand A. Patel; Wendy Stock; Sarah Monick; Thomas P. Walsh; Erin Gallagher; Marlise R. Luskin; Ana Maria Avila Rodriguez; Carlos Galvez; Peter Doukas; Jessica K. Altman; Madelyn Burkart; Amani Erra; Maryam Zia; Melissa L. Larson; Ami Dave; Stephanie B. Tsai; Ahmed Aleen; Nepheli Raptis; Christopher S. Lathan; Hajime Uno; Daniel J. DeAngelo; Gregory A. Abel

**Affiliations:** 1Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA | 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 3Department of Medicine, Northwestern University, Chicago, IL | 4Department of Medicine, The University of Chicago, Chicago, IL | 5Department of Internal Medicine, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH | 6Department of Medicine, University of Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL | 7Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Comprehensive Cancer Center, Winston-Salem, NC | 8Department of Internal Medicine, Saint Louis University, St Louis, MO | 9Department of Internal Medicine, Rush University Chicago, Chicago, IL | 10Department of Medicine, Loyola University Chicago, Maywood, IL

## Abstract

Clinical trial eligibility criteria select a target population and reduce anticipated risks for participants but may unnecessarily limit participation both overall and differently across demographic groups. We previously abstracted eligibility criteria for 190 phase 2/3 acute myeloid leukemia (AML) trials and used US Food and Drug Administration and professional society guidance on modernizing criteria to develop alternative, safety-based eligibility criteria for each trial. In this analysis, these trial- and safety-based eligibility criteria sets were applied to a retrospective cohort of 2226 newly diagnosed patients across 8 hospitals to assess the impact on eligibility. Eligibility proportions increased from a median of 47.9% with trial-based criteria to 84.2% with safety-based criteria (median difference, 30.0%; P < .001); excluding age criteria, the increase was 11.5% (P < .001). Non-Hispanic (NH) Asian, NH Black, NH White, and Hispanic patients were eligible for median proportions of 41.1%, 44.0%, 47.9%, and 50.0%, respectively, with trial-based criteria, increasing by 27.9% to 31.6% when using safety-based criteria (within-group changes, all P < .001; between-group changes, all P > .05). Excluding age criteria, increases were between 10.0% and 11.9%. Moving from trial- to safety-based criteria decreased the proportion of trials with significant eligibility differences between NH White and NH Asian (−11.1%), NH Black (−4.2%), and Hispanic (−12.1%) patients. Criteria significantly associated with increased eligibility and decreased between-group differences in eligibility were coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, aspartate transaminase level, upper age limits, and previous malignancy. These data suggest that modernization of eligibility for AML trials to focus on safety-based criteria can improve both overall enrollment and population representation.

## Introduction

Clinical trial eligibility criteria are necessary for selecting a target population and reducing anticipated or foreseeable risks for study participants. There is growing consensus that criteria may also unnecessarily limit participation in trials and do so differently across demographic groups.1-3 Although previous studies in solid tumors have suggested that site access is the major driver of decreased participation for minoritized racial and ethnic groups,4 in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), recent analyses have found that enrollment differences stem as much from differences in enrollment after patients access sites with trials as from access itself.5,6 Moreover, commonly ascribed mediators of enrollment differences, such as socioeconomic, marital status, and travel distance, were found to explain access differences but not differences in postaccess enrollment in AML, suggesting that eligibility is a major but underexplored barrier to demographic representation.

Data on eligibility criteria for patients with AML come from a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) analysis, which found that 27% of patients failed screening, and that Asian and Black patients were more frequently excluded due to organ function and mutational criteria.7 This highlights how comorbidities can cluster in certain communities and result in disproportionate exclusion when traditional eligibility criteria are applied. Yet, this analysis was limited to screened patients, included only 13 trials, and only 6% of the US cohort were from minoritized racial or ethnic groups. Relevant data from other hematologic malignancies include expert opinion–based studies in lymphoma and myelodysplastic syndromes that attempt to define which common criteria may be liberalized or eliminated,8,9 and analyses evaluating the impact of criteria on inclusion or demographic representation across small groups of trials.10,11

Despite this progress, 3 knowledge gaps remain. First, previous approaches have not systematically addressed the extent to which criteria have disproportionate impacts across groups and at the same time are overly restrictive, meaning they can be modified without exposing participants to unnecessary risk. Second, they have not addressed the impact of inconsistently applying criteria across trials (eg, using different criteria to address the same safety concern). Third, they have been restricted to a small number of trials or to a single set of criteria rather than the breadth of trials and criteria to which patients are actually exposed.

To address these gaps, we previously catalogued the actual eligibility criteria of 190 phase 2 and 3 AML clinical trials, identifying the drug safety data available at the time of study initiation and using FDA and professional society guidance12,13 to develop an alternative set of drug safety–based criteria for each trial.14 That analysis demonstrated how the actual criteria used were generally overly restrictive and applied heterogeneously across trials for the same safety signal. In this analysis, we applied the actual “trial-based” criteria and alternative “safety-based” criteria from these 190 trials to a large multicenter cohort of patients who presented with newly diagnosed AML, assessing each patient’s eligibility to each trial. We sought to determine the impact of the safety-based criteria on this population’s eligibility and whether there would have been differences in eligibility across demographic groups.

## Methods

### Study design and objectives

This multicenter retrospective cohort study counterfactually assessed patient eligibility to 190 AML clinical trials. The objectives of the study were to determine (1) eligibility overall and by race/ethnic groups using trial-based criteria, (2) differences in eligibility by race/ethnicity, (3) eligibility changes when using safety-based criteria, and (4) which criteria mediate any differences seen.

### Patients and criteria

The patient cohort included all adult patients aged 18 years and older presenting with newly diagnosed AML between 2010 and 2022 across 8 hospitals in Chicago, IL; Columbus, OH; and Boston, MA. Our previous studies show that these subcohorts are demographically representative of their respective catchment areas by race, ethnicity, age, and sex.5,15 Patient variables at the time of diagnosis were extracted from hospital medical records using automated extraction via institutional cancer registries supplemented with manual chart review. Race and ethnicity were categorized into mutually exclusive groups as Hispanic any race and non-Hispanic (NH) Asian (NHA), NH Black (NHB), NH White (NHW), and other.

Due to small numbers, individuals categorized as “other” were an aggregation of those categorized in the original data as NH Native American/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, other, more than one race, or had either race or ethnicity listed as “unknown.”

As previously described, clinical trial eligibility criteria were abstracted from 190 front-line phase 2 and/or 3 AML clinical trials active over the same period as the patient cohort, recruiting adult patients, and registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. These trials recruited a median of 52 patients (interquartile range, 27-133) and their criteria constituted the trial-based criteria used in this analysis.14 Alternative, “safety-based” criteria for each trial had also been determined previously according to the drug safety signals known at the time of study initiation and based on literature reviews according to FDA and professional society guidance.12,13 For drugs that were approved at the time of study initiation, FDA labels were reviewed for dosing, pharmacology, and safety data; Lexicomp and trials cited in the FDA label were referenced if labels were not sufficiently detailed. For drugs not approved at the time of study initiation, publicly available study protocols from earlier phase studies or studies in other settings were reviewed; PubMed.gov queries using the investigational agent name(s) were also conducted to identify additional protocols and manuscripts.

Standardized extraction templates were used for common criteria, with safety signals assigned based on information such as black box warnings, drug metabolism and elimination pathways, the prevalence and severity of related adverse events, and drug/drug interactions. The safety-based criteria for each trial were then developed by cross referencing the criteria associated with each drug tested, and the most conservative cutoff was used when a criterion was present for multiple drugs. For instance, any trial using fludarabine included a safety-based criterion of creatinine clearance of ≥30 mL/min based on the FDA label, unless another agent with a more restrictive cutoff was also used.16 Patient variables corresponding to both the trial-based and safety-based eligibility criteria are shown in supplemental Table 1 (available on the Blood website), and additional methods have been detailed and published elsewhere.14 Due to data limitations, the following variables were not included as criteria in this analysis: performance status, drug washout periods, active central nervous system disease, and use of cytoreduction.

### Statistical analysis

Demographics and clinical characteristics were descriptively summarized and differences by race/ethnic groups were assessed using χ2 or Fisher exact tests for categorical or dichotomous variables, and Kruskal-Wallis tests for numerical variables. Eligibility proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the overall cohort and by race/ethnic groups were determined for each trial and medians across all trials using trial- and safety-based criteria. The 95% CI of medians were obtained via bootstrapping, and comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Due to differences in trial size, 2 median eligibility proportions were calculated across all trials, 1 in which each trial was given the same weight (“unweighted”), and the other weighted by the anticipated number of patients enrolled (“weighted”).

Age and mutational criteria excluded substantial proportions of patients from individual trials and, because their use was not based on safety signals used to generate the safety-based criteria, led to outsized changes in eligibility between trial and safety-based criteria sets. Therefore, sensitivity analyses were performed by (1) removing the age criteria from the trial-based criteria, and (2) for the subgroup of 160 trials without mutational criteria. To determine the impact of individual criteria on (1) eligibility proportions between trial- and safety-based criteria, and (2) differences in eligibility proportions between groups, linear regression modeling was performed. For the first model, the difference in eligibility proportions between the trial- and safety-based criteria by trial was the dependent variable, and the independent variables were the individual criteria transformed into a binary variable indicating if they were less restrictive (criterion removed or cutoff liberalized) or not less restrictive (criterion unchanged, added, or cutoff more restrictive) for a given trial, and study phase was included as a covariate to assess for changes in eligibility for later phase studies. Given the large number of criteria, forward and backward stepwise model selection based on the Akaike information criterion was used for the final model.

For the second set of models, the difference in eligibility proportions between race/ethnic groups (NHW vs each other group) by trial was the dependent variable and the trial-based criteria were the independent variables; separate models were performed for each pair. To avoid overfitting with smaller numbers and to better account for imbalance in these linear regressions, significant associations in these initial multivariable linear regression models were used to select criteria for inclusion in the final models. To assess the impact of missing data, we performed multiple imputation using chained equations.17 Five imputed data sets were generated, and pooled estimates were calculated using the Rubin rules.18 For nonparametric comparisons, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were conducted within each imputed data set, and pooled P values were obtained using the median P value rule19; complete case results are reported as the primary analyses. Two-sided P < .05 was considered significant. Statistical analyses were performed using R and R-studio versions 4.3.2.

The study was approved by the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center, The Ohio State University, and University of Illinois at Chicago institutional review boards.

## Results

There were 2226 patients in the composite study cohort, with a median age of 65 years (interquartile range, 54-73), of whom 60 (2.7%) were Asian, 175 (7.9%) Black, 147 (6.6%) Hispanic, 127 (5.7%) other, and 1717 (77.1%) White. There were 789 patients (35.4%) with missing data for at least 1 criterion (supplemental Table 2). Characteristics for all patients are shown in Table 1; cases with complete and incomplete data are shown in supplemental Table 3. Those with incomplete data were more likely to be older, diagnosed in earlier years, Hispanic, have a primary language other than English, and have Medicare insurance.

Using trial-based criteria, patients were eligible for median proportions of 47.9% (unweighted; 95% CI, 46.3-50) and 48.2% (weighted by anticipated number of patients enrolled; 95% CI, 46.9-49.5) of trials overall. Using safety-based criteria, patients in the cohort were eligible for unweighted and weighted medians of 84.2% (unweighted; 95% CI, not applicable) and 91.4% (weighted; 95% CI, 91.4-91.4) of trials, or increases of 30% (57 trials; P < .001) and 35% (9430 trial slots; P < .001). The median number of criteria that excluded patients from trials are shown in Figure 1. Ineligibility heat maps by trial- and safetybased criteria are shown for each of the 190 trials in supplemental Figure 1. Without age criteria, unweighted median eligibility proportions were 65.8% (95% CI, 63.7-68.4) using trial-based criteria and 84.2% (95% CI, not applicable) using safety-based criteria; the median increase was 11.5% (22 trials; P < .001). Results for trials without mutation-based eligibility criteria were similar and are shown in supplemental Table 4.

The median proportions of trials for which patients were eligible by race/ethnic group are shown in Figure 2. According to trial-based criteria, median eligibility ranged from 41.1% for NHA patients to 50.0% for Hispanic patients, and according to safety-based criteria, median eligibility was 84.2% for all groups. Median increases in eligibility proportions by race/ethnic group when moving from trial-based to safety-based criteria were between 27.9% and 31.6% (within group differences, P < .001); without age criteria, increases were between 10.0% an 11.9% (within group differences, P < .001). Relative changes between race/ethnic groups were similar (all between-group differences, P > .05) with or without age-based criteria and are shown in supplemental Tables 5 and 6. Results for trials without mutation-based eligibility criteria are shown in supplemental Table 7.

Imputed results are shown in supplemental Tables 8 and 9. Imputed point estimates were similar to the complete case results described earlier. Owing to the more precise estimates in the imputed data set, several comparisons became significant. Notably, trial-based median eligibility proportions for NHW patients were significantly lower than for Hispanic patients (P < .001 with and without age-based criteria) and significantly higher than for NHB (P = .04 with age-based criteria).

Eligibility proportions for each trial according to trial-based and safety-based criteria are shown in Figure 3. Differences in eligibility proportions between NHW patients and each other race/ethnic group for each trial according to trial- and safety-based criteria are shown in Figure 4 and supplemental Figure 2. The proportions of trials with significant differences in eligibility by race/ethnic group according to trial-based and safety-based criteria are shown in Figure 5. Using trial-based criteria, compared with NHW patients, Black patients were significantly more or less eligible for 0.5% and 19.5% of trials, respectively, whereas Hispanic patients were significantly more or less eligible for 15.8% and 7.9% of trials, respectively. When moving from trial-based to safety-based criteria, the proportion of trials with significant differences in eligibility compared with NHW patients decreased for NHB (−4.2%), NHA (−11.1%), and Hispanic (−12.1%) patients.

Linear regressions assessing associations between differences in eligibility proportions (for individual clinical trials) between trial- and safety-based criteria sets and the restrictiveness of individual criteria are shown in Table 2 (final multivariable model) and supplemental Table 10 (univariable models). Linear regression models showing associations between differences in eligibility by race/ethnic group and eligibility criteria are shown in Table 3; results for the “other” group are shown in supplemental Table 11. Coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, aspartate transaminase level, upper age limits, and previous malignancy were significantly associated in both model types, meaning they are (1) potentially modifiable and their removal or modification leads to (2) significant increases in eligibility and (3) less differences in eligibility by race/ethnicity. Phase 3 trials, as compared with phase w trials, were associated with increased eligibility overall (Table 2) but was not significantly associated with differences in eligibility by race/ethnic group and thus not included in the Table 3 regressions. Imputed results are shown in supplemental Table 12 and had consistent results.

## Discussion

In this multicenter analysis of patient eligibility for AML clinical trials, we found there were substantial and significant increases in eligibility when criteria were modernized with a strict basis in drug safety. Applying criteria modernization also reduced both the overall differences in eligibility between race/ethnic groups and the variability of those differences across trials. We were also able to determine which criteria mediated increases in eligibility, decreases in eligibility variation across groups, or both. Together, these data demonstrate how modernizing eligibility criteria in AML can enhance population representation within and across a large number of clinical trials.

Our findings support and extend some previous findings related to eligibility criteria modernization while refuting others. Generally, these data support the premise that if eligibility criteria are aligned with safety data (ie, previous phase study results and/or FDA labels), they improve population representation compared with current practices. Although previous studies, including our own, have separately considered the safety basis of criteria,8,9,14 the effects of relaxing individual criteria,3,11 and relative impacts on demographic groups,7,10 this analysis shows these 3 effects in combination and across a population-level distribution of trials. Notably, there were absolute improvements in enrollment proportions of at least 10% (using the most conservative result) and decreased differences in eligibility across most race/ethnic groups.

We were also able to show the importance of such an approach across a large number of trials. Not only was there significant heterogeneity between actual and safety-based criteria across trials (as shown in our previous work), but a safety-based approach substantially reduced the variation in eligibility differences between demographic groups. Finally, we identified which modifiable criteria have the largest impact on population representation, which allow investigators to consider the extent to which liberalization or elimination of criteria (if based in safety) are likely to improve accrual and for which populations. Together, these insights provide actionable information for the development of more representative and generalizable AML clinical trials. This approach is transportable and can be replicated in other cancer types.

Trial generalizability is the premise that interventional clinical trials should serve as a model to determine whether an approach or treatment is or is not safe and efficacious for a population.2 Improvements in population representation through modernizing eligibility criteria not only improve the generalizability of the primary results but also the generalizability of the correlative science performed, the rate and likelihood of accrual, and patient trust in the results. There is legitimate uncertainty and expertise needed in determining what the anticipated or foreseeable risks are, and which are acceptable for participants. This is evidenced by the increased eligibility proportions for phase 3 studies seen in this analysis. Notably, however, there were relatively few studies with phase 3 portions (n = 32), which reflects the market trend of using phase 2 studies as the basis for accelerated FDA approval followed by delayed (or omitted) phase 3 testing.20,21 The substantial heterogeneity of criteria across trials, and the consistent gaps between trial and real-world outcomes,22 also highlight the extent to which changes in criteria are both possible and, arguably, necessary.

This study’s approach, taken intentionally, did not assess the relationship between eligibility and survival. Undoubtedly, such a relationship exists, but other studies have assessed this as a way to show if and how criteria changes are based in safety, and we believe that that approach is flawed. Implicitly, such an approach argues that decreased survival with criteria modernization may be less safe for patients although it is just as likely to reflect how restrictive criteria succeed in selecting an artificially healthier group that does not reflect the population with the disease. Recent findings highlight this artificial restrictiveness. A study by Orcutt et al found that even among real-world patients who appear the most similar to trial participants and are treated with the same regimen, 75% have inferior survival compared to the trial population.22 In the context of trial-based care itself having limited associations with survival,23 this strongly suggests selection bias among the trial population. Given the high rate of single-arm phase 2 trials that benchmark their end points to historical controls, less restrictive inclusion criteria may lead to reduced survival. This should be addressed during end point selection and, more broadly, highlights the limitations of historical controls and the rationale for performing randomized rather than single-arm phase 2 trials.

This work is situated in a field in which there is growing recognition of the interplay between molecular, demographic, and social, and treatment factors. This analysis identified several associations between recurrent mutations and changes in eligibility that bring to mind recent findings of differential mutational prevalence, risk, and treatment outcomes by race or genetic ancestry.24,25 That said, the numbers of trials and patients with these mutations were low overall, leading to imprecise estimates that warrant dedicated study. Also, although this study assesses trial eligibility, there are genetic ancestral associations with diagnostic criteria and response definitions that could be evaluated using similar methods for their biologic rationale and safety basis. A key example is Duffy null phenotype’s differential distribution by race, which affects the absolute neutrophil counts used to define remission in AML and other blood cancers.26,27 The integration of molecular, clinical, and social factors is only just beginning.

This study has limitations. Although our patient data source was relatively large, included multiple institutions, and generally reflected the AML population in the National Cancer Institute–designated catchment areas of those institutions,5,15 the data were obtained retrospectively and subject to the limitations of variable and data incompleteness and heterogeneity. The locations of the involved sites and the average age of the population studied make these findings potentially less generalizable to populations from rural locations, those in the south and western United States enriched for Hispanic and Asian populations, studies at sites with different demographic mixes, and younger adults. The development of safety-based criteria, although done rigorously and according to external standards provided by the FDA and American Society of Clinical Oncology,1,13 may not have captured unpublished safety data. The use of race/ethnicity as the basis for generalizability also only serves as a proxy for other aspects of generalizability such as health care access, socioeconomic status, cultural practices and beliefs, and structural racism. Although the intent of this study was not to assess the contribution of these mediating factors to any differences seen, these are important factors that affect eligibility, directly or indirectly, that should be further studied.

This multicenter analysis of patient eligibility to AML clinical trials found that substantial increases in eligibility could be obtained when criteria are modernized according to drug safety data. Application of modernized criteria also led to lower eligibility differences between demographic groups both overall and for individual trials. This approach also identified which criteria had the greatest impact, highlighting an actionable path toward improved AML trial generalizability. Because FDA and American Society of Clinical Oncology guidance are imperfectly reflected in current trials,28 future work should test interventions that can modernize new studies during development. This includes external review of draft criteria, updating clinical trial templates and instructions for institutional review board reviewers, obtaining input from community advisors, and training investigators and sponsors. Our data can serve as an important guidepost for such interventions, which can, in turn, lead to optimally safe and generalizable AML clinical trials.
